# Inspect Linux pinctrl ownership
$ mount -t debugfs none /sys/kernel/debug 2>/dev/null
$ cat /sys/kernel/debug/pinctrl/*/pinmux-pins 2>/dev/null
$ cat /sys/kernel/debug/pinctrl/*/pins 2>/dev/null

# Search logs for pinctrl and peripheral errors
$ dmesg | grep -Ei 'pinctrl|gpio|spi|i2c|uart|can'

data.content_0_12_0:
1. Identify the exact PHYTEC board, SoM, processor, revision and BSP release.
2. Find the signal and its electrical requirements in the PHYTEC documents.
3. Read the exact SoC reference manual register fields.
4. Use the BSP pinctrl header and existing DTS examples.
5. Separate mux selection from pad electrical configuration.
6. Check external pulls, voltage rails, loads, level shifters and termination.
7. Choose the least aggressive valid drive and slew setting first.
8. Review default, idle and sleep pinctrl states.
9. Build and verify the deployed DTB and live pinctrl ownership.
10. Measure the signal when needed; record the final value, reason and evidence.
data.content_0_1_1: The names and available bits differ between NXP and TI. Some settings are represented by macros; others are encoded in a hexadecimal value. Always use the definitions supplied for the exact SoC.
data.content_0_5_4: When reviewing a value, write down the intended electrical meaning in plain English. For example: “No internal bias, input enabled, medium drive, slow slew.” Do not rely on the hexadecimal number alone.

data.danger_0_13_1: Do not write unknown register values or use an incompatible voltage setting. Incorrect electrical configuration can damage hardware or create unsafe contention.

data.important_0_4_2: The same hexadecimal number can mean different things on different i.MX families. Read the matching `imx*-pinfunc.h` definitions and reference manual.
data.important_0_6_2: TI offset and bit definitions differ between AM62x, AM64x, AM68x and other K3 devices. Use the exact binding, header and SoC documentation.
data.important_0_9_5: A peripheral can work in the default state and still fail during suspend, resume or runtime power management if the sleep state is wrong.

data.main_content_0_0: A processor pin is more than a name in a device tree. It is connected to a pad cell with a mux selector and electrical controls. The mux selects which internal peripheral reaches the pad. Pad controls affect how the signal behaves electrically, such as input enable, pull resistors, drive strength and slew rate.
data.main_content_0_10: Prefer the Linux pinctrl debug information and source definitions. Direct register reads can help during expert debugging, but reading or writing an address without the exact SoC manual can be unsafe.
data.main_content_0_13: Pinmux registers connect Linux configuration to real electrical behavior. The mux selects the internal function, while pad-control fields define input behavior, bias, drive and edge speed. NXP and TI encode these settings differently, so the exact SoC reference manual and PHYTEC board design must guide every value. Use symbolic macros and existing BSP patterns where possible, verify the live pinctrl state, and measure the signal when software evidence is not enough. This verification process confirms the deployed result.
data.main_content_0_2: Mux control answers: “Which function is connected to this pad?” Pad control answers: “How should this electrical connection behave?” These are related but separate decisions.
data.main_content_0_3: Use the following order when choosing a value: the PHYTEC hardware manual and schematic, the exact SoC reference manual, the BSP pinctrl header and existing board DTS examples. A random internet example is not an authority.
data.main_content_0_4: NXP i.MX Linux device trees commonly use `fsl,pins`. An entry normally contains a symbolic pad/mux macro followed by a pad-control value. The macro selects the pad and function; the value configures electrical behavior according to the exact i.MX family.
data.main_content_0_5: Depending on the i.MX family, pad-control fields can include pull configuration, pull/keeper behavior, drive strength, slew rate, open-drain selection and hysteresis. The bit positions and legal combinations are not universal.
data.main_content_0_6: TI K3 Linux device trees commonly use `pinctrl-single,pins`. A pin entry contains a register offset and a value written to the pin configuration register. PHYTEC trees may use TI macros to make the SoC-specific offset and mode easier to read.
data.main_content_0_7: Drive strength controls the output current capability. Slew rate controls how quickly the output changes voltage. More drive and faster slew are not automatically better: they can increase ringing, overshoot, crosstalk and electromagnetic interference.
data.main_content_0_8: Open-drain buses such as I2C use devices that pull the line low while an external resistor returns it high. Both SDA and SCL need the correct input/output behavior. Reset, interrupt and GPIO lines can also be bidirectional or open-drain depending on the circuit.
data.note_0_13_0: Hexadecimal pad-control values have meaning only for the exact SoC family and register definition that owns them.

data.sub_content_0_6_3: TI pad configuration may include input enable, pull enable, pull direction, drive strength, slew rate and mux mode. The available fields depend on the pad and device family. Some signals have special requirements in the TI technical reference manual.
data.sub_content_0_6_6: A pull resistor is a weak default bias used when no stronger device is driving the line. It can keep a GPIO, reset line or bus signal at a known level. It is not a replacement for a required external resistor on every interface.
data.sub_content_0_9_0: The SoC setting is only one part of the circuit. PHYTEC boards may include level translators, external pull resistors, series resistors, ESD components, multiplexers or onboard peripherals.
data.sub_content_0_9_2: Linux can select different pinctrl states for active use, idle use and sleep. A low-power state may change pulls or output levels. Review all states, not only the `default` group.
data.tip_0_0_2: A correct mux can still produce a bad signal if the voltage domain, pull resistor, drive strength or slew rate is wrong.
data.tip_0_7_2: Use an oscilloscope or logic analyzer when the software configuration looks correct but the signal is unreliable. A register dump alone cannot show waveform quality.
data.warning_0_10_2: Do not use a raw register write as a permanent fix. It disappears on reboot and can interfere with drivers, power management or another peripheral.
data.warning_0_2_1: Changing a pad-control value does not select a peripheral. Changing only the mux does not guarantee a reliable electrical signal.
data.warning_0_5_1: Do not enable an internal pull against a strong external driver. This can waste current, distort a bus or create contention.
data.warning_0_6_8: Never assume “pull-up” or “pull-down” is safe from the signal name alone. Check the peripheral datasheet, PHYTEC schematic and power-up behavior.
